recipes.name: BREAK starts a fresh 77-token chunk
recipes.claim: BREAK starts a fresh 77-token chunk; weighting (token:1.3) scales the token's embedding vector — and the two interact (weights can't cross a BREAK boundary).
recipes.summary: ComfyUI/A1111 chunk long prompts into 75-content-token blocks; BREAK force-ends the current chunk and pads it, then concats per-chunk embeddings. Weighting: A1111-style scales the token's CLIP embedding vector magnitude (multiply by the weight, lerp from zero vector); ComfyUI default instead lerps the embedding between the prompt and an empty prompt — so identical (token:1.3) syntax produces DIFFERENT strengths across UIs. Optional normalization (mean / length / length+mean) restores overall embedding magnitude after weighting so heavy weights don't blow out the whole conditioning. A weight on a token sitting at a chunk boundary behaves unpredictably because emphasis can't reach across the boundary.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: Use BREAK to isolate subjects and kill color bleed (one subject+palette per chunk); keep each chunk a self-contained <=75-token unit. Keep weights modest: 1.05-1.3 up, 0.7-0.9 down; >1.4 fries the embedding (deep-fried look). Standardize the studio on ONE UI's weighting interpretation (or ComfyUI's AdvancedCLIPEncode in A1111-compat + a fixed normalization) so saved weights mean the same thing run-to-run. Never put a weighted token right at a BREAK boundary.

recipes.name: Even within 77 tokens, CLIP's EFFECTIVE length is only ~20…
recipes.claim: Even within 77 tokens, CLIP's EFFECTIVE length is only ~20 tokens — content after position ~20 contributes weakly and unreliably.
recipes.summary: Long-CLIP measured that CLIP retrieval (R@1) stops growing meaningfully once input exceeds ~20 tokens, because CLIP's training captions were short, so only the first ~20 positional embeddings were trained enough to indicate absolute position; positions 21-77 give only a rough relative estimate. This is a TRAINING-DATA artifact, not a soft architectural taper — the back half of even a legal-length prompt is mush.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Treat the first ~20 tokens as the only positions that reliably bind. Front-load: [subject] + [1-2 defining attributes] + [medium/style] in tokens 1-20. Demote nice-to-haves (background, secondary props) to later positions and EXPECT them to be soft. If a detail MUST appear, it belongs in the first 20 tokens or in its own BREAK chunk, not buried at token 60.

recipes.name: SDXL runs TWO CLIP encoders in parallel and concatenates them
recipes.claim: SDXL runs TWO CLIP encoders in parallel and concatenates them — 768d (CLIP-L) + 1280d (bigG) = 2048d per token, plus a 1280d pooled vector from bigG only.
recipes.summary: Both encoders tokenize the same prompt independently with the same 77-token CLIP tokenizer. Their penultimate-layer per-token hidden states are concatenated along the channel axis (768+1280=2048) and fed to the UNet cross-attention. Separately, bigG's pooled (single end-of-text) embedding (1280d) conditions the UNet globally. There is no learned reconciliation between the two encoders' readings — they are literally glued side by side, so a prompt that one encoder parses cleanly and the other garbles produces a blended/muddy concept.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Write ONE clean prompt that both encoders can read (plain, depictable, well-ordered) rather than tricks tuned for one. SDXL lets you send different text to encoder 1 vs encoder 2 (A1111 'AND'-style / ComfyUI CLIPTextEncodeSDXL dual fields), but as a default keep them identical; only split them when you have a deliberate reason (e.g. style tags in one, subject in the other) and A/B test it — divergent dual prompts are a known source of mush.

recipes.name: CLIP encodes concrete visual words robustly but…
recipes.claim: CLIP encodes concrete visual words robustly but abstract/non-visual words inconsistently — the brittleness is word-TYPE-specific, not random.
recipes.summary: Karthik et al. show CLIP text encoders are 'brittle': semantically-equivalent paraphrases and reorderings produce divergent embeddings, AND the divergence is far larger for abstract/emotional/non-visual tokens than for concrete depictable nouns/adjectives. Concrete visual words (objects, colors, materials, observable actions) land in stable, well-separated regions of the embedding space; abstract words ('grief', 'guarded', 'regulation-issue') map to mushy, overlapping regions with no consistent visual referent, because CLIP's contrastive objective only ever rewarded text that matched pixels. An abstract token therefore contributes a near-arbitrary direction to the conditioning vector — it does not encode 'nothing', it encodes noise.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Every adjective/noun in the prompt must name something a camera could photograph. Replace 'worn by grief' → 'dark circles under eyes, downturned mouth, slumped shoulders'; 'guarded' → 'arms crossed, chin lowered, narrowed eyes'; 'regulation-issue jacket' → 'plain olive-drab jacket, brass buttons'. If you cannot point to the pixel it changes, cut the word.

recipes.name: Describe what is VISIBLE, not what is TRUE' is forced by…
recipes.claim: 'Describe what is VISIBLE, not what is TRUE' is forced by reporting bias in the training captions — the encoder literally never learned to depict inferred/contextual facts.
recipes.summary: Onoe-style reporting-bias work shows web captions (LAION etc.) follow Grice's maxim: humans omit the visually obvious and instead report the noteworthy/inferred ('parked at the beach', 'after the funeral') rather than 'a red car, four doors, chrome trim'. So the encoder's training signal systematically UNDER-represents plain visible attributes and contains almost no signal linking causal backstory to pixels. A token like 'the patch is faded because he stopped caring' has no learned visual consequence — the 'because he stopped caring' half is invisible to the model. The fix is not better phrasing of the intent; it is replacing intent with its visible RESULT.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Write the screenshot, not the script. For each canon fact, ask 'what would a frame-grab show?' Backstory ('faded because neglected') → visible result ('faded, frayed-edge cloth patch, loose thread'). Emotion ('worn by grief') → visible result ('red-rimmed eyes, three-day stubble, stained collar'). Never prompt causation, intent, history, or off-screen truth.

recipes.name: T5-XXL (FLUX/Chroma) gives token-level structure and…
recipes.claim: T5-XXL (FLUX/Chroma) gives token-level structure and handles long depictable descriptions — but it is text-only, so it still cannot ground abstract intent; longer just means more room for visible detail, not for backstory.
recipes.summary: In FLUX, CLIP-L supplies only a single pooled global vector (scale/shift modulation) while T5-XXL supplies the fine-grained per-token features the U-Net actually cross-attends to. T5 keeps word order and clause structure (unlike bag-of-words CLIP), so it binds attributes and follows compositional phrasing far better — this is why FLUX rewards natural-language, comma-light, descriptive prose. BUT T5 is trained on pure text (Raffel 2020): it knows 'grief co-occurs with crying' linguistically, yet has zero pixel grounding, so it routes that as a vague statistical nudge, not a depiction. The studio's mushy result is exactly this: T5 happily encoded the grief-prose into a real-valued direction with no visual target, diluting the depictable tokens it was concatenated with.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: For FLUX/Chroma, write fluent descriptive sentences but fill them ONLY with visible specifics: 'A weathered man in a faded olive jacket with a frayed cloth patch on the left shoulder; deep under-eye shadows, three-day stubble, jaw set, gaze lowered.' Use the longer budget to add MORE visible attributes (lighting, material, framing, pose), never to add mood/history. Put the most load-bearing visual subject early.

recipes.name: CLIP's effective attention dies around token ~20, not token 77
recipes.claim: CLIP's effective attention dies around token ~20, not token 77 — late tokens are near-invisible even before truncation.
recipes.summary: Long-CLIP shows CLIP's absolute positional embeddings beyond ~position 20 are undertrained (training captions were short), so retrieval/conditioning strength flatlines after ~20 tokens. The 77-token cap is a hard ceiling, but the SOFT ceiling is ~20. In SDXL this hits both CLIP-L and bigG, and bigG's pooled-embedding global-gist path is dominated by the earliest high-salience tokens. A face descriptor buried at token 40 of an SDXL prompt is effectively whispered.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: On SDXL, front-load face/identity descriptors into the FIRST ~10-15 tokens: e.g. 'sharp detailed face, [hair/eye/age], <character>, full-body, ...' NOT '...wandering a ruined keep at dusk, full-body, worn cloak, ... detailed face'. If you need a long SDXL prompt, use BREAK to start a fresh 75-token chunk so the face descriptor sits early in its own chunk.

recipes.name: Identity does NOT come from the text encoder
recipes.claim: Identity does NOT come from the text encoder — face-preservation methods explicitly bypass text because CLIP/T5 features are too coarse for precise ID.
recipes.summary: InstantID states CLIP 'features predominantly capture broad, ambiguous semantic information like composition, style, and colors... they fall short for tasks requiring precise ID preservation,' and instead injects a face embedding from a dedicated face-recognition model (ArcFace/antelopev2). IP-Adapter-FaceID likewise swaps the CLIP image embedding for an ArcFace face embedding for the identity channel, routed through a DECOUPLED cross-attention path separate from text. So a specific hero's likeness can never live in the prompt string — text only controls everything AROUND the identity (pose, outfit, lighting, scene).  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Never try to pin a recurring hero's exact likeness with words. Get likeness from a reference plate via IP-Adapter-FaceID / InstantID (ArcFace embedding); use the text prompt only for pose, framing, wardrobe, lighting, and mood. Words like 'detailed face' improve fidelity-of-rendering, not identity-match — keep those two jobs separate in your head.

recipes.name: SDXL feeds TWO 77-token CLIP encoders whose token features…
recipes.claim: SDXL feeds TWO 77-token CLIP encoders whose token features are concatenated to [B,77,2048] plus a pooled global embedding — so it is doubly biased toward early, high-salience tokens.
recipes.summary: SDXL runs CLIP-L and OpenCLIP-bigG independently, concatenates their penultimate-layer token features channel-wise into a [B,77,2048] tensor, and ADDITIONALLY conditions on bigG's pooled text embedding. Both encoders share the 77-cap / ~20-effective falloff, and the pooled path summarizes the whole prompt into one vector dominated by salient early tokens. Net: SDXL has the least room of any encoder here for a face to compete with a busy scene description.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: On SDXL treat the prompt as ~15 high-value tokens, face-first, and offload everything else: put scene/atmosphere mood into the negative-space of a second BREAK chunk, and let likeness come from IP-Adapter/InstantID rather than burning precious early tokens trying to word-paint a specific face. Do not write 60-token SDXL character prompts and expect the face clause at the end to land.

recipes.name: Both Qwen encoders are NATIVELY bilingual (CN/EN) and read…
recipes.claim: Both Qwen encoders are NATIVELY bilingual (CN/EN) and read on-image TEXT as literal glyphs — a capability CLIP/T5 lack and a structural reason word-for-word quoting works.
recipes.summary: Qwen-Image's system prompt explicitly asks the encoder to detail 'text' of objects, and the model card markets 'Excellent Multilingual Text Rendering' (EN/CN/KR/JP/IT). Z-Image's paper cites Qwen3-4B's 'bilingual proficiency.' Because the encoder is a real language model, text you want rendered IN the image should be quoted verbatim; the encoder tokenizes it as literal characters the DiT then draws — unlike CLIP, where text rendering is incidental and unreliable.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: To render words in the image, put them in straight quotes exactly as they should appear: a chalkboard reading 'Qwen Coffee'. For CJK output, write the prompt (and the magic tail) in that language — don't prompt in English and hope for Chinese signage. This is a genuine capability lift over the CLIP/T5 stack; use it.

recipes.name: Padding behavior differs
recipes.claim: Padding behavior differs: Qwen-Image pads to a uniform length; Z-Image FILTERS padding by default — short prompts can be 91% padding, so structure matters more than you'd think.
recipes.summary: Qwen-Image masks then pads to a uniform sequence length for batching. Z-Image's reference path sets filter_padding=True, stripping padding tokens before the DiT (matching diffusers/DiffSynth) — and the docs note a short prompt can be ~91% padding. Practically this means very short Z-Image prompts give the DiT very few real conditioning tokens, so each word you spend is high-leverage, and front-loading the subject matters even more on short prompts.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: On Z-Image, don't pad your own prompt with filler hoping to 'fill the context' — padding is filtered anyway. Spend tokens on real visual content. If a prompt is very short, every adjective counts; if it's long, keep the load-bearing subject in the first ~30% of tokens so it survives any tail truncation.

recipes.name: Qwen-Image's REAL token budget is huge vs CLIP/T5
recipes.claim: Qwen-Image's REAL token budget is huge vs CLIP/T5: 1024-token hard ceiling, 512 default — roughly 13x CLIP's 77 and 2x FLUX-dev's T5 512.
recipes.summary: tokenizer_max_length=1024 is the hard cap; the __call__ default max_sequence_length=512. About 34 tokens are consumed by the (stripped) system span. Compare: CLIP-L/bigG truncate hard at 77 tokens (ComfyUI fakes longer prompts by chunking into 75-token blocks and concatenating); FLUX/Chroma's T5-XXL caps at 512 (256 on Schnell). So Qwen-Image genuinely ingests paragraph-length prompts in one coherent causal pass, with no chunk seams.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: You can safely write 2-4 sentence prompts for Qwen-Image (aim under ~480 tokens / ~1900 English chars to stay inside the 512 default; raise max_sequence_length toward 1024 only if you genuinely need it). Stop translating CLIP-era brevity habits — but every token past the limit is silently dropped from the TAIL, so never bury the key subject at the end.

recipes.name: Z-Image wraps prompts in a chat template and can run a…
recipes.claim: Z-Image wraps prompts in a chat template and can run a <think> reasoning block (enable_thinking) — reasoning/knowledge is offloaded to a SEPARATE Prompt Enhancer VLM, not the encoder.
recipes.summary:
The reference template is '<|im_start|>user
{}<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant
' (matching diffusers with enable_thinking=True default); an optional system block '<|im_start|>system
{content}<|im_end|>' can be prepended. But the paper is explicit that heavy lifting is a module, not the encoder: 'we propose equipping Z-Image with a Prompt Enhancer (PE), powered by system prompt and a pretrained VLM, to improve its reasoning and knowledge capabilities.' So the raw Qwen3-4B encoder is NOT where you put a paragraph expecting reasoning — that's the PE's job.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: For Z-Image, either (a) let the official Prompt Enhancer expand a short seed concept, OR (b) feed an already-detailed, self-contained visual description — but do NOT hand the raw encoder a terse cryptic prompt and expect it to reason out the scene; it won't, the PE does. If you bypass the PE, write the full description yourself.

recipes.name: Distilled/turbo models ignore negative prompts because…
recipes.claim: Distilled/turbo models ignore negative prompts because guidance is baked into a SINGLE forward pass — there is no second (unconditional/negative) branch for the negative to occupy.
recipes.summary: Guidance distillation (FLUX-dev, FLUX-schnell, SDXL-Turbo/Lightning, LCM, Z-Image-Turbo) trains the student to reproduce, in one forward pass, what a teacher produced with a full CFG two-pass extrapolation. FLUX-dev does this by feeding the guidance value itself as a conditioning embedding (guidance_embeds=true) rather than running two passes; FLUX-schnell drops it entirely. Practically these models run at effective cfg_scale=1, where eps_guided = eps_uncond + 1*(eps_cond - eps_uncond) = eps_cond — the uncond/negative term mathematically vanishes. There is literally no negative branch being evaluated, so a negative_prompt string is inert (often silently accepted and discarded by the UI). Running a real CFG>1 on these models doubles compute AND breaks the distilled output, which is why guides say 'set CFG=1, do not use a negative prompt' for FLUX-dev/schnell.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: On Z-Image-Turbo, FLUX-dev, FLUX-schnell, SDXL-Turbo/Lightning, LCM: stop writing negative prompts — they do nothing. Put ALL steering in the POSITIVE prompt (describe the flat cel look you WANT, not the realism you don't). If a UI lets you raise CFG on a turbo model, leave it at 1; raising it fries the image and slows generation for no benefit.

recipes.name: NAG (Normalized Attention Guidance) restores real…
recipes.claim: NAG (Normalized Attention Guidance) restores real negative-prompt control on distilled/turbo models by doing the extrapolation in ATTENTION space instead of in the noise prediction.
recipes.summary: NAG (Chen et al. 2025, arXiv:2505.21179) is training-free. Inside attention, it computes positive and negative attention features Z+ and Z-, extrapolates Z_tilde = Z+ + scale*(Z+ - Z-), then applies L1-based normalization (a tau clamp that constrains how far Z_tilde may deviate from Z+) and alpha-blends back toward Z+. The normalization is the key trick: naive attention extrapolation drifts out-of-manifold (the same divergence that kills CFG in few-step models), and the L1 clamp keeps it stable. NAG is validated on FLUX-schnell (4-step), FLUX-dev, SDXL-Turbo/DMD2, SD3.5-Large-Turbo, and Wan2.1 video; on FLUX-schnell 4-step it improves CLIP score +2.1 and cuts FID 18% vs no guidance. Recommended nag_scale ~5 for FLUX/SD3.5-Turbo and ~3 for SDXL-DMD2, with guidance_scale left at 0.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: If the studio wants negative-prompt control on Z-Image-Turbo / FLUX-schnell-class models, add the NAG node (ComfyUI) or NAG-enabled pipeline and put suppressions (e.g. 'blurry, realistic, watermark, extra fingers') in nag_negative_prompt with nag_scale ~3-5. This is the ONLY mechanically valid way to get negative-like control on a distilled model — a plain negative_prompt field on those models is still a no-op.

recipes.name: Distilled/turbo models (FLUX-dev, FLUX-schnell,…
recipes.claim: Distilled/turbo models (FLUX-dev, FLUX-schnell, Z-Image-Turbo, SDXL-Turbo/Lightning) have no true CFG, so the negative field is dead weight -- and a non-empty negative can actively cost speed for zero benefit.
recipes.summary: Guidance distillation bakes the guidance behavior into the weights; inference runs a single conditional pass with a 'distilled guidance' scalar (FLUX-dev default ~3.5), not the two-pass cond/uncond subtraction CFG requires. With CFG=1 there is no uncond/negative branch to substitute, so the negative is ignored by design (Forge greys out the negative field at CFG=1). Schnell doesn't even use guidance. Re-enabling real CFG to force a negative (e.g. via dynamic-thresholding hacks or pseudo-negative nodes) roughly doubles step cost and breaks the distillation the model was trained for. (This restates the established rule; the actionable payoff is the cleanup instruction.)  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: On FLUX-dev/schnell, Z-Image-Turbo, SDXL-Turbo/Lightning: leave the negative field EMPTY. Put avoid-intent into the positive as presence-language ('clean uncluttered background, sharp focus'). Do not wire CFG-restoring negative hacks for production art -- they ~2x cost for marginal gain.

recipes.name: A negative prompt is a CONCEPT to move away from, not a…
recipes.claim: A negative prompt is a CONCEPT to move away from, not a sentence containing a negation -- put 'hat', not 'no hat'.
recipes.summary: CFG (Ho & Salimans 2022) computes output = uncond + scale*(cond - uncond); negative prompting replaces the uncond branch with the negative embedding, so the sampler is mechanically pushed DOWN the gradient of whatever the negative text encodes. The field already means 'away-from'. Words like 'no'/'without'/'not' are near-meaningless to the image encoders (CLIP has no robust logical negation; T5 spreads attention contextually) so 'no hat' encodes the concepts {no, hat} and the dominant token is 'hat' -- you push away from the negation word's neighborhood while still naming the thing. arXiv:2601.08070 (Semantic Gravity Wells) shows the 'priming' failure mode dominates: explicitly naming the forbidden token in a negation construction is itself the primary risk factor (87.5% of failures), because attention lands on the named target, not the negation cue.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Write bare depictable concept tokens in the negative field: 'hat, sunglasses, blur'. NEVER write 'no hat' or 'without a hat'. The field sign already handles the 'no'.

recipes.name: Negatives bite LATE in sampling and only after the positive…
recipes.claim: Negatives bite LATE in sampling and only after the positive has rendered content -- so a negative cannot pre-empt a defect, it can only correct an emerging one.
recipes.summary: arXiv:2406.02965 measures the timing: positive prompts attend to their content in the first ~4 steps, but negative prompts cannot align to the target region until step ~8+, peaking around step 5 for noun removal and plateauing around step 10 for adjective/quality refinement; they are effectively inert after ~step 11. This is why a negative reliably removes an object that the positive is trying to draw (object cancellation) but is a poor tool for shaping global composition or 'baking in' style -- those decisions are already locked in the first few steps. Practical implication: negatives are a corrective scalpel, not a steering wheel.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Use negatives to remove/clean specific emergent elements (an unwanted object, blur, a watermark), NOT to set composition or style -- do that in the positive. Don't expect a negative to fix something decided in the first 4 steps.

recipes.name: Even the SD1.5 negative embeddings are ANIME-trained on…
recipes.claim: Even the SD1.5 negative embeddings are ANIME-trained on specific checkpoints and carry style baggage — they are not neutral 'quality boosters.'
recipes.summary: EasyNegative was trained WITH the Counterfeit anime checkpoint (8 vectors) and is intended for anime models (Anything v3, OrangeMix); its own README says 'effectiveness is not certain' on other models. ng_deepnegative and the bad-hands family are likewise anime-finetune artifacts. Because a TI embedding is a learned shortcut into ONE model's latent space, applying it elsewhere injects that model's aesthetic bias, not generic 'quality.' For a commercial 2.5D JRPG painterly/illustrative house style this is a style-contamination risk even where it loads, pulling toward generic anime rendering.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: Do not treat negative embeddings as model-agnostic quality dials. If you ever use one (SD1.5 only), assume it injects the aesthetic of its training checkpoint (Counterfeit/anime) and A/B it against your locked style plate before trusting it. For a defined commercial art style, prefer an explicit, auditable text negative over an opaque embedding whose training data you can't inspect.

recipes.name: A negative prompt is literally the CFG unconditional term…
recipes.claim: A negative prompt is literally the CFG unconditional term replaced by a conditioned term — it only exists because CFG subtracts it; with no real CFG it does nothing.
recipes.summary: CFG (Ho & Salimans 2022) computes the final noise as eps_uncond + scale*(eps_cond - eps_uncond). The community swap is: feed the negative prompt as the 'uncond' branch, so the model is pushed AWAY from eps_neg by exactly (scale-1). This is the entire mechanism. At CFG=1 the (eps_cond - eps_uncond) term vanishes and the negative branch is never evaluated — which is why FLUX-dev/schnell, Z-Image-Turbo, and SDXL-Turbo/Lightning (guidance-distilled, run at CFG≈1) silently discard any negative_prompt. The 'distilled/Flux guidance' slider is a baked-in scalar, NOT a second conditioning pass, so there is no eps_neg to subtract.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Only fill negative_prompt on un-distilled CFG models (base SDXL ~CFG 5-8, Chroma, Qwen-Image base). On FLUX-dev/schnell, Z-Image-Turbo, SDXL-Turbo/Lightning leave negative empty — every token you put there is dead weight that costs encode time and zero effect. If you genuinely need negative steering on FLUX, you must add a true-CFG node (real second pass), accepting ~2x compute.

recipes.name: Quality-WORD negatives ('worst quality, low quality,…
recipes.claim: Quality-WORD negatives ('worst quality, low quality, lowres, normal quality') are a booru-finetune artifact and are PLACEBO on non-anime / photoreal / painterly bases.
recipes.summary: Tags like 'masterpiece / worst quality / low quality' fire on anime models because Danbooru/booru training data was literally tagged with those quality buckets — the model learned a real association between the token and image quality. Photoreal and many painterly/illustrative bases were NOT trained on that tag vocabulary, so the token has no learned referent and steering is near-zero ('placebo' per practitioner consensus). For a 2.5D JRPG built on SDXL photoreal/painterly checkpoints (not a booru finetune), copying anime quality-negatives in adds dilution (see finding 2) for no benefit.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: Only use 'worst quality/low quality/masterpiece'-style quality tags if your specific checkpoint is a booru/anime finetune that was TRAINED on them — verify by ablation. On photoreal or painterly JRPG bases, drop quality-word negatives entirely and negate concrete visual artifacts you actually see (e.g. 'jpeg artifacts', 'oversharpened halos') instead.

recipes.name: Before rewriting a prompt for a 'missing element', check CFG
recipes.claim: Before rewriting a prompt for a 'missing element', check CFG — under-guidance reads as a prompt miss but is fixed by the guidance scale, not re-wording. Over-guidance burns quality and faces.
recipes.summary: Classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans, arXiv 2207.12598) sets how hard the model is pushed toward the conditioning by extrapolating between the conditional and unconditional predictions at each step. Too low, and requested elements get under-expressed or dropped — which mimics a prompt failure even though the prompt is fine. Too high, and you get oversaturation, mode collapse, and degraded/melted faces — which mimics a seed/instance failure even though the prompt is fine. CFG is therefore a third axis that masquerades as both: a missing-element symptom is sometimes a guidance floor problem, and an ugly-instance symptom is sometimes a guidance ceiling problem. It must be ruled out before you spend edits on either the seed or the prompt wording. Note FLUX-family models use a distilled/embedded guidance that behaves differently from SDXL's CFG scale — the principle holds, the dial doesn't transfer.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: When an element is faint or dropped, before rewording: nudge CFG UP a notch (locked seed, locked prompt) and see if it appears — under-guidance, not a prompt miss. When faces/skin look fried or oversaturated, nudge CFG DOWN before blaming the seed — over-guidance, not an unlucky instance. Only after CFG is dialed correctly do you decide seed vs prompt. (FLUX/Chroma: use their guidance-embedding dial, not SDXL CFG values.)

recipes.name: Once the prompt is RIGHT, run a BATCH of N seeds to explore…
recipes.claim: Once the prompt is RIGHT, run a BATCH of N seeds to explore composition — that's the legitimate, productive use of re-rolling.
recipes.summary: After the conditioning reliably produces the right kind of output, the remaining variation (pose, framing, face, hand layout) is pure z_T lottery, and the correct move is to sample that lottery in bulk rather than one-at-a-time. The Diffusers workflow is explicitly two-phase: first generate a batch with a LIST of generators (one seed each), then lock onto the winner. In production this is throughput discipline: a batch of 8-16 seeds on a fixed good prompt surfaces the best instance far faster than serial single re-rolls, and because each image is tied to exactly one reproducible seed, the winner is re-summonable for downstream variation (expressions, angles) by holding its seed and editing the prompt.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: When the defect is composition (not content), do NOT re-roll one seed at a time — fire a batch of 8-16 seeds against the FROZEN prompt in a single run, with each image bound to its own logged seed. Pick the winner by eye, record its seed number, then iterate. Batching is the seed-side tool; reserve serial single re-rolls for nothing.

recipes.name: Whether a defect is even seed-fixable depends on the text…
recipes.claim: Whether a defect is even seed-fixable depends on the text encoder. CLIP (SDXL) drops attributes and mis-binds adjectives as a STRUCTURAL limit — re-rolling never fixes a CLIP binding miss; switch tactics (or model) instead.
recipes.summary: SDXL conditions on CLIP encoders that behave bag-of-words cross-modally: with multiple objects, an adjective routinely binds to the wrong noun or is ignored ('red sword, blue cloak' yields a blue sword), and negation/counting fail. This is an encoder property, invariant to the seed — so on SDXL, an attribute-binding or missing-element miss is firmly prompt-side and often needs structural fixes (split into regional prompts, reduce competing attributes, reorder, reweight) rather than re-wording alone. T5/LLM-conditioned models (FLUX, Chroma, Qwen-Image) have markedly stronger natural-language adherence and longer token budgets, so a miss that is hopeless to seed-fix on SDXL may simply be a wording fix there. The seed-vs-prompt decision is the same everywhere; the PROMPT ceiling — how much the prompt can be trusted to land — moves with the encoder.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: On SDXL/CLIP: treat any attribute-binding or missing-element miss as encoder-structural — do NOT re-roll and do NOT just re-word; reduce competing attributes, use regional/split prompting, reorder so the key noun+adjective lead, and reweight. On FLUX/Chroma/Qwen: a content miss is more often a plain wording/specificity fix — rewrite naturally and verify with a locked-seed A/B before batching.

recipes.name: Exact reproducibility requires the WHOLE stack to match,…
recipes.claim: Exact reproducibility requires the WHOLE stack to match, not just the seed: same model, sampler, steps, CFG, resolution, scheduler, AND node graph — plus same GPU architecture and library versions for bit-exactness.
recipes.summary: The seed is one of ~6 generation parameters; change any of model/sampler/steps/CFG/resolution and the image changes despite the seed. Bit-exact reproduction additionally needs matching hardware: different GPU architectures (e.g. Pascal vs Turing) 'deviate a lot' on both noise generation and downstream compute, and non-deterministic kernels (xformers/CUTLASS) break determinism even within one machine. So 'I used the same seed' guarantees nothing on its own.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: To reliably re-generate a hero asset, archive the FULL recipe: model hash + sampler + steps + CFG + resolution + scheduler + the exact node graph/workflow JSON + seed (and note the GPU). Store the ComfyUI workflow embedded in the PNG. Do NOT expect to reproduce a shot from the seed alone, and don't expect bit-identical output across machines or after a library upgrade. For a commercial pipeline, pin the workflow file as the source of truth, with the seed as just one field in it.

recipes.name: A good seed does NOT survive a resolution change. Changing…
recipes.claim: A good seed does NOT survive a resolution change. Changing width or height — even by a few pixels — reshapes the noise tensor, so the same seed yields a different noise pattern and a different image.
recipes.summary: Resolution is the SHAPE of the latent noise tensor (e.g. 4x64x64 for 512x512, 4x96x64 for a portrait). The seed fills that tensor element-by-element; change the tensor dimensions and the RNG fills a differently-shaped array, producing fundamentally different noise. There is no meaningful correspondence between 'seed 469 at 1024x1024' and 'seed 469 at 832x1216'. Tools' 'seed resize' features only approximate visual similarity and explicitly fail with ancestral samplers.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: Lock your generation resolution BEFORE seed-sweeping for a character shot. Never sweep at low res then bump resolution expecting the same composition — re-sweep at the final resolution, or generate at the locked res and upscale via img2img / Hires-fix / a dedicated upscaler (which preserves the image, not the seed). For a portrait pipeline, pick one canonical aspect ratio per shot type and freeze it.

recipes.name: CFG controls HOW HARD the prompt steers the trajectory away…
recipes.claim: CFG controls HOW HARD the prompt steers the trajectory away from the unconditional (seed-only) direction -- it is the prompt's volume knob, not a content knob.
recipes.summary: CFG = eps_uncond + w*(eps_cond - eps_uncond). At w=1 the prompt barely steers (you drift toward the seed's generic unconditional reconstruction -> bland). Raising w pushes harder toward the prompt manifold (more literal adherence) but too-high w over-saturates, fries detail, and collapses diversity. Low CFG = creativity/seed dominates; high CFG = prompt dominates literally. Crucially, CFG cannot inject information the prompt never stated -- it can only amplify the steering force of whatever IS in the prompt.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: If the model is IGNORING a good detailed prompt (you described the scar, it has no scar), nudge CFG up before re-rolling. If results look fried/over-contrasted/plasticky, lower CFG. But if the prompt is vague, raising CFG just makes a generic image more aggressively generic -- fix the prompt first, CFG second, seed third.

recipes.name: The sampler determines the PATH from the seed's noise to…
recipes.claim: The sampler determines the PATH from the seed's noise to the image; ancestral (stochastic) samplers inject fresh noise each step, so they partly override the seed's determinism.
recipes.summary: Given a fixed seed (z_T) and prompt, the sampler chooses the integration path of the reverse ODE/SDE. Deterministic samplers (DDIM, Euler, DPM++ 2M) follow a fixed path -> same seed reproduces exactly and converges as steps increase. Ancestral/SDE samplers (Euler a, DPM++ SDE) add NEW random noise at every step, so the same seed + same prompt can yield different images at different step counts and never fully 'settle.' This means with Euler a, some apparent variation is sampler stochasticity, not the seed.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: For reproducible character iteration where you want the SEED to be the only variable, use a deterministic sampler (DDIM / Euler / DPM++ 2M). Reserve ancestral samplers (Euler a) for when you WANT extra variety. If you are A/B testing prompt edits, a deterministic sampler isolates the prompt's effect cleanly; an ancestral one muddies it.

recipes.name: Seeds DO vary in quality, but that quality is largely…
recipes.claim: Seeds DO vary in quality, but that quality is largely PROMPT-SPECIFIC, not a portable 'magic number' -- the magic-seed folklore is partly real, mostly false.
recipes.summary: Empirically, seeds are not equal: across 1,024 seeds, a 'golden' seed reached FID 21.60 vs an 'inferior' seed's 31.97 (Good Seed Makes a Good Crop); compositional accuracy swung 41.0% vs 28.3% across seeds for multi-object prompts (All Seeds Are Not Equal). A classifier can ID the generating seed with >99.9% accuracy -- seeds leave a structural fingerprint. BUT: there is no correlation between the seed NUMBER and the output, and a seed's goodness does not reliably transfer to a different subject/prompt. So 'seed 12345 is lucky for everything' is FOLKLORE; 'for THIS prompt, some noise samples place the figure better than others' is real.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Do not hoard 'magic seeds' as portable assets across characters -- a good seed for one prompt is not good for another. The legit move: once your PROMPT is dialed, batch 4-8 seeds and curate the best composition/pose; pin that seed for THAT exact prompt for reproducibility. Never use a fixed favorite seed as a substitute for writing a strong prompt.

recipes.name: CLIP's effective attention span is ~20 tokens, not 77
recipes.claim: CLIP's effective attention span is ~20 tokens, not 77 — front-load the subject and key visual attributes.
recipes.summary: CLIP was trained on short web captions, so position embeddings beyond ~20 tokens are under-trained; empirically CLIP's effective length is ~20 tokens and self-attention is biased toward early tokens. The 77-token cap is a hard ceiling, but tokens 21-75 carry weak, degraded signal even when not truncated. This is the single most important structural fact for SDXL prompting.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: On SDXL (and the CLIP-L side of FLUX), put the subject + 3-5 highest-priority visual attributes in the FIRST ~20 tokens (~75-90 chars). Everything after token ~20 is decoration with diminishing returns. Lead with 'weary female knight, faded green tabard, short silver hair' — never bury the subject behind quality words or mood.

recipes.name: masterpiece / best quality / very aesthetic' work ONLY on…
recipes.claim: 'masterpiece / best quality / very aesthetic' work ONLY on Danbooru-trained anime bases — on base SDXL/FLUX/Qwen they are folklore filler.
recipes.summary: Anime fine-tunes (Pony, Animagine, Illustrious, NoobAI) were trained with explicit quality-tier tags ('masterpiece', 'best quality', score_9) as learned conditioning, so those tokens genuinely shift output quality on THOSE models. Base SDXL, FLUX, Chroma, Qwen-Image, and Z-Image never saw that vocabulary as a quality signal — the words are just generic tokens that consume budget (and on CLIP, burn precious early-token positions). Carrying them onto a photoreal/JRPG-painterly base is cargo-cult.  [grounding: folklore-DEBUNKED]
recipes.design_implication: Use quality tags ('masterpiece', 'best quality', 'score_9') ONLY when the checkpoint is a Danbooru/booru-tag anime fine-tune that documents them. On base SDXL, FLUX, Chroma, Qwen-Image, Z-Image: drop them and instead name concrete style descriptors the model actually learned ('hand-painted 2.5D JRPG key art, soft rim light, gouache texture'). Never spend CLIP's first 20 tokens on 'masterpiece, best quality.'

recipes.name: T5-based diffusion models (FLUX, Chroma) do NOT respond to…
recipes.claim: T5-based diffusion models (FLUX, Chroma) do NOT respond to non-depictable / narrative tokens — prose like 'worn by grief' is dead weight that dilutes the visual tokens.
recipes.summary: Although T5 was trained on the C4 natural-language corpus full of abstract text, diffusion models conditioned on T5 simply do not act on non-visual prompts — the visual-relevant subspace of T5's embedding is small and the rest is redundant for image synthesis. Abstract/backstory tokens still consume the token budget and shift the mean of the conditioning, pulling the image toward a generic average. This is the direct mechanism behind the studio's 'mushy generic' failure.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: For T5 encoders, write ONLY depictable facts. Convert every emotional/backstory clause into its visual consequence: NOT 'worn by grief, guarded and steady' but 'hollow cheeks, dark under-eye shadows, jaw set, eyes narrowed, shoulders squared.' NOT 'a patch faded because of a long war' but 'sun-bleached frayed shoulder patch, threadbare edges.' If a token can't be drawn, delete it.

recipes.name: Longer prose helps T5 only up to a concrete-detail ceiling
recipes.claim: Longer prose helps T5 only up to a concrete-detail ceiling; padding it with narrative prose past ~70-90 dense visual words gives diminishing returns and can dilute, not enrich.
recipes.summary: T5 genuinely follows detailed natural-language descriptions (unlike CLIP), so concrete added detail helps — up to a point. Community/vendor guidance converges on a sweet spot well below the token cap (commonly ~30-80 words for the core, dense visual content), with the observation that beyond a few hundred words effective signal saturates and competing clauses smear attributes. The 512-token cap is headroom for DETAIL, not an invitation to write a paragraph of story.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: Aim for a dense, all-visual paragraph in the 60-150 word range for a single character/sprite; every word should name something the camera could see. Use the remaining T5 budget for concrete specifics (materials, colors, lighting, lens) — not narrative. If quality drops when you lengthen, CUT rather than add.

recipes.name: On T5, punctuation is SEMANTIC
recipes.claim: On T5, punctuation is SEMANTIC: commas vs periods change style, and proper sentence punctuation steers interpretation — the opposite of CLIP where commas are just separators.
recipes.summary: Because T5 parses real grammar, the Chroma/Lodestone guidance reports that comma-chaining tags biases toward cartoon/anime, while period-separated tags and full sentences bias toward realism/photo. Sentence structure (subject-verb-object, prepositional phrases) is how T5 binds attributes to the right object — the mechanism CLIP lacks. Chroma additionally is un-distilled and supports real CFG + NEGATIVE prompts (FLUX-dev/schnell are distilled and ignore negatives), so on Chroma you also have a working negative channel to push out unwanted traits.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: For realistic 2.5D sprites on Chroma/FLUX, write full sentences and separate trailing tags with PERIODS (commas pull toward anime/cartoon). Use grammar to bind attributes ('a girl with a red cloak and a silver sword', not 'red, cloak, silver, sword, girl'). On Chroma specifically, move 'remove this' content into the negative_prompt — it actually works there; on FLUX-dev/schnell negatives are ignored, so don't rely on them.

recipes.name: Weighting/emphasis syntax
recipes.claim: Weighting/emphasis syntax — (token:1.3), ((token)) — is largely FOLKLORE on T5 pipelines; T5 has no native attention-weighting and the SDXL-era syntax does not transfer.
recipes.summary: Attention/emphasis syntax was built for the CLIP-based SD/SDXL stack (where UIs rescale CLIP token embeddings). T5 produces contextual sentence embeddings with no per-token weight knob; in pure diffusers there is no parser for (word:1.2). ComfyUI applies its weighting hack to the CLIP stream, but it does not meaningfully reweight T5, and Flux's strong native prompt-adherence makes the trick low-value at best and quality-damaging at worst. Emphasis on T5 is achieved by WORDING, position, and repetition of the concept in plain language — not punctuation.  [grounding: folklore-DEBUNKED]
recipes.design_implication: Do NOT use (word:1.4) / ((word)) weighting in FLUX/Chroma T5 prompts. To emphasize a trait, state it earlier, state it more specifically, or restate it as a second plain-language clause ('a scarred face; the scar runs from brow to jaw'). Reserve numeric weighting for the SDXL/CLIP lane only.
